claim: Malaria accounts for approximately 200 million cases annually, with 600,000 deaths.
source: Malaria is one of the world's three major infectious diseases, together with AIDS and tuberculosis, accounting for approximately 200 million cases annually, with 600,000 deaths (Snow et al., 2005; Murray et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Snow et al., 2005 and Murray et al., 2012.

claim: Antibodies play a major role in the protective immunity directed against the blood-stage malaria parasite.
source: Antibodies play a major role in the protective immunity directed against the blood-stage malaria parasite.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: CD4+ T cells contribute to protection against blood-stage malaria through induction of antibody production and macrophage activation.
source: CD4+ T cells contribute to protection against blood-stage malaria though induction of antibody production and macrophage activation (Good and Doolan, 1999; Marsh and Kinyanjui, 2006; Jafarshad et al., 2007; Langhorne et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The contribution of CD8+ T cells to protection against blood-stage malaria remains controversial because there are no major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I antigens on human erythrocytes infected with the malaria parasite.
source: However, the contribution of CD8+ T cells to this protection remains controversial because there are no major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I antigens on human erythrocytes infected with the malaria parasite.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about human erythrocytes and the basis for controversy.

claim: Infection of BALB/c mice with non-lethal Plasmodium yoelii was controlled even after depletion of CD8+ T cells comparable to control mice.
source: Some studies have shown that infection of BALB/c mice with non-lethal Plasmodium yoelii was controlled even after depletion of CD8+ T cells comparable to control mice (Vinetz et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vinetz et al., 1990.

claim: MHC class I null mice (beta 2-microglobulin-deficient mice) recovered from infection with Plasmodium chabaudi chabaudi AS or Plasmodium chabaudi adami.
source: Moreover, MHC class I null mice (beta 2-microglobulin-deficient mice) recovered from infection with Plasmodium chabaudi chabaudi AS or Plasmodium chabaudi adami (van der Heyde et al., 1993b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to van der Heyde et al., 1993b.

claim: Depletion of CD8+ T cells from mice infected with P. chabaudi attenuated their protection, confirming the importance of CD8+ T cells.
source: Other studies have reported that depletion of CD8+ T cells from mice infected with P. chabaudi attenuated their protection, confirming the importance of CD8+ T cells (Suss et al., 1988; Podoba and Stevenson, 1991; van der Heyde et al., 1993a; Horne-Debets et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The transfer of CD8+ T cells from mice cured of PyNL infection into Rag2−/− or irradiated recipients, followed by two boosts with PyL, conferred protection against PyL.
source: The transfer of CD8+ T cells from mice cured of PyNL infection into Rag2−/− or irradiated recipients, followed by two boosts with PyL, conferred protection against PyL.
evidence: This is a statement of experimental results from the authors' previous work.

claim: The major protective mechanism of CD8+ T cells is the interferon γ (IFN-γ)-dependent activation of phagocytes, resulting in the enhanced phagocytosis of parasitized red blood cells (pRBCs).
source: The major protective mechanism of CD8+ T cells is the interferon γ (IFN-γ)-dependent activation of phagocytes, resulting in the enhanced phagocytosis of parasitized red blood cells (pRBCs).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The cytotoxic activity of CD8+ T cells also contributes to protecting the host against blood-stage malaria.
source: The cytotoxic activity of CD8+ T cells also contributes to protecting the host against blood-stage malaria.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The human malaria parasites Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax parasitize erythroblasts.
source: Although recent reports have demonstrated that the human malaria parasites Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax parasitize erythroblasts (Ru et al., 2009; Tamez et al., 2009), the host response and protective immunity against these parasitized erythroblasts are unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ru et al., 2009 and Tamez et al., 2009.

claim: PyNL parasites infect erythroblasts that express MHC class I molecules on their surfaces.
source: We have reported that PyNL parasites also infect erythroblasts that express MHC class I molecules on their surfaces and that CD8+ T cells produce IFN-γ in response to parasitized erythroblasts in an antigen-specific manner.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: CD8+ T cells produce IFN-γ in response to parasitized erythroblasts in an antigen-specific manner.
source: We have reported that PyNL parasites also infect erythroblasts that express MHC class I molecules on their surfaces and that CD8+ T cells produce IFN-γ in response to parasitized erythroblasts in an antigen-specific manner.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: C57BL/6 mice infected with PyNL exhibited peak parasitemia of up to 30% and recovered from the infection.
source: C57BL/6 mice infected with PyNL exhibited peak parasitemia of up to 30% and recovered from the infection.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments described.

claim: C57BL/6 mice depleted of CD8+ T cells showed significantly greater parasitemia and died from PyNL infection.
source: However, those depleted of CD8+ T cells showed significantly greater parasitemia and died from the infection (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BALB/c mice depleted of CD8+ T cells showed significantly greater parasitemia and died from PyNL infection.
source: BALB/c mice depleted of CD8+ T cells showed similar results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that CD8+ T cells play an essential role in protecting mice against blood-stage malaria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD8+ T cells play an essential role in protecting mice against blood-stage malaria.
source: BALB/c mice depleted of CD8+ T cells showed similar results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that CD8+ T cells play an essential role in protecting mice against blood-stage malaria.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing increased parasitemia and mortality in CD8+ T cell-depleted mice.

claim: CD4+-T-cell-depleted mice displayed greater parasitemia and a higher mortality rate.
source: We confirmed that CD4+-T-cell-depleted mice displayed greater parasitemia and a higher mortality rate (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The course of infection clearly differed in CD8+-T-cell-depleted and CD4+-T-cell-depleted mice.
source: However, the course of infection clearly differed in CD8+-T-cell-depleted and CD4+-T-cell-depleted mice.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the experimental data.

claim: Mice depleted of CD8+ T cells suffered from much greater parasitemia from the early phase to its peak, but survivors eliminated the parasites similar to the control mice.
source: Although mice depleted of CD8+ T cells suffered from much greater parasitemia from the early phase to its peak, the survivors eliminated the parasites similar to the control mice, whereas the CD4+-T-cell-depleted survivors took longer to recover from infection.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: CD4+-T-cell-depleted survivors took longer to recover from infection.
source: Although mice depleted of CD8+ T cells suffered from much greater parasitemia from the early phase to its peak, the survivors eliminated the parasites similar to the control mice, whereas the CD4+-T-cell-depleted survivors took longer to recover from infection.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells have different effector mechanisms for parasite clearance.
source: This suggests that CD4+ and CD8+ T cells have different effector mechanisms for parasite clearance, and that the protective immunity mediated by CD8+ T cells is important in controlling infection during the early phase, within the period of peak parasitemia.
evidence: This is inferred from the different infection courses observed in CD4+ and CD8+ T cell-depleted mice.

claim: The protective immunity mediated by CD8+ T cells is important in controlling infection during the early phase, within the period of peak parasitemia.
source: This suggests that CD4+ and CD8+ T cells have different effector mechanisms for parasite clearance, and that the protective immunity mediated by CD8+ T cells is important in controlling infection during the early phase, within the period of peak parasitemia.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD8+ T cell-depleted mice show greater parasitemia early in infection.

claim: PyNL infection increased the proportion of CD8+ T cells that expressed activation markers such as CD25 and CD69.
source: PyNL infection increased the proportion of CD8+ T cells that expressed activation markers such as CD25 and CD69 (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CD8+ T cells started to express the cytotoxicity-related molecules FasL and LAMP1 after PyNL infection.
source: and the CD8+ T cells started to express the cytotoxicity-related molecules FasL (Krueger et al., 2003) and lysosome-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) (Wolint et al., 2004) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B and citations indicating these are cytotoxicity-related molecules.

claim: The course of infection in gld mice resembled that in mice depleted of CD8+ T cells, with exacerbated parasitemia before peak parasitemia and lower survival rate than in wild-type mice.
source: The course of infection in the gld mice resembled that in mice depleted of CD8+ T cells, insofar as parasitemia was exacerbated before peak parasitemia and the survival rate was lower than in wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: FasL is important in controlling blood-stage malaria.
source: Thus, FasL is important in controlling blood-stage malaria.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FasL-mutant gld mice show similar infection course to CD8+ T cell-depleted mice.

claim: Infection did not increase the expression of FasL on CD4+ T cells, in contrast to CD8+ T cells.
source: However, this is unlikely because infection did not increase the expression of FasL on CD4+ T cells, in contrast to CD8+ T cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CD8+ and CD4+ T cells isolated from mice that had recovered from PyNL infection after two homologous boosts with PyL transferred protection from an otherwise lethal infection with PyL to the recipient mice.
source: To confirm these inferences, we used cell transfer experiments combined with a prime–boost live vaccination system in which CD8+ and CD4+ T cells isolated from mice that had recovered from PyNL infection after two homologous boosts with PyL transferred protection from an otherwise lethal infection with PyL to the recipient mice (Figure 1E,F) (Imai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F and citation to Imai et al., 2010.

claim: Mice that had received gld immune CD8+ T cells exhibited higher parasitemia at an early stage of infection, and some of them failed to control the challenge infection and died.
source: Mice that had received gld immune CD8+ T cells exhibited higher parasitemia at an early stage of infection, and some of them failed to control the challenge infection and died (Figure 1F, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CD4+ T cells from gld donors protected the recipients from challenge with PyL, similar to the protection afforded mice by CD4+ T cells from WT donors.
source: In contrast, CD4+ T cells from gld donors protected the recipients from challenge with PyL, similar to the protection afforded mice by CD4+ T cells from WT donors (Figure 1F, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FasL plays a crucial role in CD8+-T-cell-mediated protective immunity against blood-stage malaria.
source: Therefore, FasL plays a crucial role in CD8+-T-cell-mediated protective immunity against blood-stage malaria.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gld CD8+ T cells fail to provide full protection while gld CD4+ T cells retain protective capacity.

claim: CD8+ T cells obtained from 'immune' CD45.1-bearing C57BL/6 mice could transfer protection to Rag2−/− mice (CD45.2).
source: CD8+ T cells obtained from 'immune' CD45.1-bearing C57BL/6 mice could transfer protection to Rag2−/− mice (CD45.2), although parasitemia was greater compared with when the irradiated mice were used as hosts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, Imai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and citation to Imai et al., 2010.

claim: The ratio of the contaminated CD4+ cells in sorted CD8+ cells used for the transfer was less than 0.1%.
source: The ratio of the contaminated CD4+ cells in sorted CD8+ cells used for the transfer was less than 0.1% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The ratio of contaminated CD4+ cells in donor-derived CD45.1+ cells recovered from the recipients did not exceed 0.8%, and CD8+ T cells constantly occupied more than 96% even after infection with PyNL.
source: That in donor-derived CD45.1+ cells recovered from the recipients did not exceed 0.8%, and CD8+ T cells constantly occupied more than 96% even after infection with PyNL (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The recipients transferred with 1 × 10^7 CD4+ T cells could control the challenge infection, but those with 1 × 10^6 CD4+ T cells could not.
source: The recipients transferred with 1 × 107 CD4+ T cells could control the challenge infection, but those with 1 × 106 CD4+ T cells could not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: 0.1% contaminated CD4+ T cells corresponding to 1 × 10^4 in transferred 10^7 CD8+ T cells seem to have no protective ability.
source: Thus, 0.1% contaminated CD4+ T cells corresponding to 1 × 104 in transferred 107 CD8+ T cells seem to have no protective ability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 1 × 10^6 CD4+ T cells cannot control infection, so 1 × 10^4 would be insufficient.

claim: CD8+ T cells are responsible for the transferred protection.
source: Based on these findings, we concluded that CD8+ T cells are responsible for the transferred protection.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing minimal CD4+ T cell contamination and their insufficient numbers to provide protection.

claim: Erythroid cells express Fas.
source: Recently, erythroid cells have been reported to express Fas (De Maria et al., 1999; Tsushima et al., 1999; Mandal et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Malaria parasites infect erythroblasts.
source: Based on our previous finding that malaria parasites infect erythroblasts (Imai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Very few TER119+ erythroid cells expressed Fas in the peripheral blood, even among the infected GFP+ cells.
source: Very few TER119+ erythroid cells expressed Fas in the peripheral blood, even among the infected GFP+ cells (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A number of infected GFP+ cells expressing Fas were present in the spleen, and the frequency of those cells among the parasitized cells reached 50% before peak parasitemia.
source: In contrast, a number of infected GFP+ cells expressing Fas were present in the spleen, and the frequency of those cells among the parasitized cells reached 50% before peak parasitemia (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Almost all Fas-expressing cells, both infected and uninfected, were MHC class I^hi.
source: Almost all Fas-expressing cells, both infected and uninfected, were MHC class Ihi (Figure 2C), indicating that the infected Fas+ cells were erythroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The infected Fas+ cells were erythroblasts.
source: Almost all Fas-expressing cells, both infected and uninfected, were MHC class Ihi (Figure 2C), indicating that the infected Fas+ cells were erythroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fas+ cells are MHC class I^hi, which is a marker of erythroblasts.

claim: The infection of erythroblasts with PyNL may induce their expression of Fas.
source: Notably, the infection of erythroblasts with PyNL may induce their expression of Fas, because Fas− erythroblasts were markedly reduced in the infected cells relative to their numbers in uninfected cells (41% and 14%, respectively; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fas− erythroblasts are reduced among infected cells compared to uninfected cells.

claim: The intensity of Fas expression was much higher on parasitized erythroblasts than in uninfected erythroblasts.
source: Moreover, the intensity of Fas expression was much higher on parasitized erythroblasts than in uninfected erythroblasts.
evidence: This is an observation from the flow cytometry data.

claim: PS+ cells were significantly increased in splenic infected TER119+ cells.
source: PS+ cells were significantly increased in splenic infected TER119+ cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CD8+-T-cell-depleted or gld mice had much fewer PS+ cells than the control mice.
source: CD8+-T-cell-depleted or gld mice had much fewer PS+ cells than the control mice (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The majority of infected Fas+ splenic erythroblasts displayed PS.
source: Moreover, the majority of infected Fas+ splenic erythroblasts displayed PS (Figure 3D), suggesting that CD8+ T cells and FasL are involved in increasing the exposure of PS on infected cells in the spleen.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CD8+ T cells and FasL are involved in increasing the exposure of PS on infected cells in the spleen.
source: Moreover, the majority of infected Fas+ splenic erythroblasts displayed PS (Figure 3D), suggesting that CD8+ T cells and FasL are involved in increasing the exposure of PS on infected cells in the spleen.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that PS+ cells are reduced in CD8+ T cell-depleted and gld mice.

claim: The number of PS+ cells among the infected RBCs was only slightly increased in the peripheral blood.
source: In contrast, the number of PS+ cells among the infected RBCs was only slightly increased in the peripheral blood.
evidence: This is an observation from the flow cytometry data.

claim: The increase in PS+ cells in peripheral blood seemed to be dependent on FasL and CD8+ T cells, despite the absence of Fas+ cells in the peripheral blood.
source: Because the gld and CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice contained fewer PS+ infected RBCs, the increase in PS+ cells seemed to be dependent on FasL and CD8+ T cells, despite the absence of Fas+ cells in the peripheral blood.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gld and CD8+ T cell-depleted mice have fewer PS+ infected RBCs.

claim: CD8+ T cells from infected WT mice efficiently induced PS exposure in a dose-dependent manner.
source: CD8+ T cells from infected WT mice efficiently induced PS exposure in a dose-dependent manner, whereas those from uninfected WT mice did not (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CD8+ T cells from uninfected WT mice did not induce PS exposure.
source: CD8+ T cells from infected WT mice efficiently induced PS exposure in a dose-dependent manner, whereas those from uninfected WT mice did not (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Exposure of PS was only observed in infected GFP+ cells, and not in uninfected cells.
source: Exposure of PS was only observed in infected GFP+ cells, and not in uninfected cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CD8+ T cells from infected gld mice induced PS exposure in only a few infected GFP+ cells, as did the CD8+ T cells from uninfected WT mice.
source: Importantly, CD8+ T cells from infected gld mice induced PS exposure in only a few infected GFP+ cells, as did the CD8+ T cells from uninfected WT mice (Figure 4B,C), indicating that FasL expressed by CD8+ T cells is responsible for PS exposure.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: FasL expressed by CD8+ T cells is responsible for PS exposure.
source: Importantly, CD8+ T cells from infected gld mice induced PS exposure in only a few infected GFP+ cells, as did the CD8+ T cells from uninfected WT mice (Figure 4B,C), indicating that FasL expressed by CD8+ T cells is responsible for PS exposure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gld CD8+ T cells fail to induce PS exposure.

claim: The addition of FasL–Strep induced the externalization of PS in infected GFP+ cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The addition of FasL–Strep induced the externalization of PS in infected GFP+ cells in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The PS+ cells were all MHC class I^hi erythroblasts, even in the absence of FasL–Strep.
source: The PS+ cells were all MHC class Ihi erythroblasts, even in the absence of FasL–Strep (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: FasL–Strep reduced the proportion of MHC class I^hi erythroblasts in PS− cells (from 64% to 50%).
source: Furthermore, FasL–Strep reduced the proportion of MHC class Ihi erythroblasts in PS−cells (from 64% to 50%), indicating that PS− Fas-expressing erythroblasts expose PS in the presence of FasL–Strep (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PS− Fas-expressing erythroblasts expose PS in the presence of FasL–Strep.
source: Furthermore, FasL–Strep reduced the proportion of MHC class Ihi erythroblasts in PS−cells (from 64% to 50%), indicating that PS− Fas-expressing erythroblasts expose PS in the presence of FasL–Strep (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MHC class I^hi erythroblasts decrease in the PS− population after FasL–Strep treatment.

claim: PS exposure was not observed on infected cells from the peripheral blood, even in the presence of CD8+ T cells or FasL–Strep.
source: In contrast, PS exposure was not observed on infected cells from the peripheral blood, even in the presence of CD8+ T cells or FasL–Strep (Figure 5), presumably because Fas was not expressed on these cells (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PS was only displayed on infected erythroid cells when the erythrocytes contacted CD8+ T cells, and was not affected by soluble factors secreted from CD8+ T cells.
source: Transwell experiments revealed that PS was only displayed on infected erythroid cells when the erythrocytes contacted CD8+ T cells, and was not affected by soluble factors secreted from CD8+ T cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by Transwell experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Activated CD8+ T cells can induce PS exposure on infected splenic cells (parasitized erythroblasts) in a FasL- and contact-dependent manner during blood-stage malaria.
source: These results indicate that activated CD8+ T cells can induce PS exposure on infected splenic cells (parasitized erythroblasts) in a FasL- and contact-dependent manner during blood-stage malaria, although the involvement of exosomes bearing pro-apoptotic membranous FasL could not be ruled out (Andreola et al., 2002).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of the experiments showing FasL-dependence and contact-dependence.

claim: Mice depleted of macrophages by administration with clodronate/liposome (C/L) quickly died in association with high parasitemia.
source: In line with previous reports from ourselves and others on the importance of the phagocytosis of infected RBCs in the protective response to blood-stage malaria (Zhang et al., 1999; Couper et al., 2007; Imai et al., 2010; Matsuzaki-Moriya et al., 2011; Duan et al., 2013), mice depleted of macrophages by administration with clodronate/liposome (C/L) quickly died in association with high parasitemia (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B and citations to prior research.

claim: PS-exposing cells are highly susceptible to phagocytosis by macrophages.
source: It has also been reported that PS-exposing cells are highly susceptible to phagocytosis by macrophages (Fadok et al., 1998; van den Eijnde et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fadok et al., 1998 and van den Eijnde et al., 1998.

claim: Only a few macrophages phagocytosed the uninfected cells, whereas up to 30% of macrophages engulfed the infected cells from the WT mice.
source: Only a few macrophages phagocytosed the uninfected cells, whereas up to 30% of macrophages engulfed the infected cells from the WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phagocytosis assay data.

claim: When cocultured with infected cells from CD8+-T-cell-depleted WT or gld mice, the number of phagocytotic macrophages was significantly reduced.
source: When cocultured with infected cells from CD8+-T-cell-depleted WT or gld mice, the number of phagocytotic macrophages was significantly reduced (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A positive correlation between the degree of PS exposure on the infected cells and the numbers of phagocytotic macrophages was observed.
source: A positive correlation between the degree of PS exposure on the infected cells and the numbers of phagocytotic macrophages was observed, indicating that PS+ cells are readily phagocytosed (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: PS+ cells are readily phagocytosed.
source: A positive correlation between the degree of PS exposure on the infected cells and the numbers of phagocytotic macrophages was observed, indicating that PS+ cells are readily phagocytosed (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is inferred from the positive correlation between PS exposure and phagocytosis.

claim: Substantial numbers of infected cells were phagocytosed in the spleen but not in the peripheral blood.
source: Substantial numbers of infected cells were phagocytosed in the spleen but not in the peripheral blood, indicating the importance of this organ in the elimination of the malaria parasite (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The spleen is important in the elimination of the malaria parasite.
source: Substantial numbers of infected cells were phagocytosed in the spleen but not in the peripheral blood, indicating the importance of this organ in the elimination of the malaria parasite (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that phagocytosis occurs primarily in the spleen.

claim: The proportion of phagocytosed infected cells in the total infected cells (CD11b+ GFP+/GFP+) in the spleens of CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice was significantly lower than the proportion in the control mice.
source: The proportion of phagocytosed infected cells in the total infected cells (CD11b+ GFP+/GFP+) in the spleens of CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice was significantly lower than the proportion in the control mice (Figure 8A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A,B,D.

claim: gld mice showed similar results to those of CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice in terms of phagocytosis of infected cells.
source: Furthermore, gld mice showed similar results to those of CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: F4/80+ red pulp macrophages are responsible for the ingestion of parasites.
source: Finally, we analyzed macrophage subsets and found that F4/80+ red pulp macrophages are responsible for the ingestion of parasites.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of macrophage subsets.

claim: SIGNR1+ marginal zone macrophages, CD169+ marginal metallophilic macrophages, and CD68+ tingible-body macrophages appeared not to be involved in phagocytosis.
source: SIGNR1+ marginal zone macrophages, CD169+ marginal metallophilic macrophages, and CD68+ tingible-body macrophages appeared not to be involved in phagocytosis (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Depletion of CD8+ T cells did not affect the numbers of each macrophage subset.
source: Although depletion of CD8+ T cells did not affect the numbers of each macrophage subset (data not shown), it dramatically reduced the number of phagocytic F4/80 macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Depletion of CD8+ T cells dramatically reduced the number of phagocytic F4/80 macrophages.
source: Although depletion of CD8+ T cells did not affect the numbers of each macrophage subset (data not shown), it dramatically reduced the number of phagocytic F4/80 macrophages.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The macrophages in the CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice were activated to a similar degree as those in the control mice during malaria.
source: As the macrophages in the CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice were activated to a similar degree as those in the control mice during malaria (Figure 9), the proportion of cells exposing PS may correspond to this difference in the number of phagocytosing macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The proportion of cells exposing PS may correspond to the difference in the number of phagocytosing macrophages.
source: As the macrophages in the CD8+-T-cell-depleted mice were activated to a similar degree as those in the control mice during malaria (Figure 9), the proportion of cells exposing PS may correspond to this difference in the number of phagocytosing macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that macrophage activation is similar but phagocytosis differs.

claim: The phagocytosis of infected cells occurs in the spleen and correlates with the exposure of PS on the infected cells, which is dependent on CD8+ T cells and FasL.
source: These results indicate that the phagocytosis of infected cells occurs in the spleen and correlates with the exposure of PS on the infected cells, which is dependent on CD8+ T cells and FasL.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the combined experimental results.

claim: Tim-4 was identified as a PS receptor.
source: Recently, T-cell immunoglobulin- and mucin-domain-containing molecule (Tim-4; also known as Timd4) was identified as a PS receptor (Miyanishi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Miyanishi et al., 2007.

claim: The expression of Tim-4 on splenic macrophages was upregulated, and the number of Tim-4+ macrophages increased in response to infection with PyNL.
source: The expression of Tim-4 on splenic macrophages was upregulated, and the number of Tim-4+ macrophages increased in response to infection with PyNL (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The phagocytosis by macrophages of infected RBCs isolated from infected WT mice was dose-dependently inhibited by the presence of antibodies directed against Tim-4.
source: The phagocytosis by macrophages of infected RBCs isolated from infected WT mice was dose-dependently inhibited by the presence of antibodies directed against Tim-4 (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phagocytosis inhibition assay data shown in Figure 10B,C.

claim: Tim-4 contributes to the phagocytosis of infected RBCs.
source: These results indicate that Tim-4 contributes to the phagocytosis of infected RBCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that anti-Tim-4 antibodies inhibit phagocytosis.

claim: CD8+ T cells interact with infected erythroblasts and induce them to display PS in a FasL-dependent manner.
source: Here, we have demonstrated a novel protective mechanism against blood-stage malaria conferred by CD8+ T cells. CD8+ T cells interact with infected erythroblasts and induce them to display PS in a FasL-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: PS exposure enhances the susceptibility of infected cells to phagocytosis, which contributes to the elimination of the parasite.
